query: How to implement Olofsson et al. (2014) area-estimation for an 11-class stratified map and compute unbiased area estimates, variances, and 95% CIs?

response.query: How to implement Olofsson et al. (2014) area-estimation for an 11-class stratified map and compute unbiased area estimates, variances, and 95% CIs?
response.answer: Implement stratified random sampling, calculate unbiased area estimates using post-stratification, and compute variances and 95% CIs using the methods described by Olofsson et al. (2014).

results.title: Forest dynamics mapping in central Vietnam from 1988 to 2022 using Landsat time-series data
results.content: Five LULC classes—undisturbed forest, disturbed forest, cropland, water, and non-vegetated—were identified based on land cover research (Nguyen and Nguyen 2022) and official Vietnamese classifications (Portal of Huế 2016, Duong _et al_2021) (see table 1). The forest mask was then integrated with the forest disturbance map and the ‘Undisturbed’ class from the LULC map to generate the final forest change map for each period, following the stratified mapping approach recommended by Olofsson _et al_ (2014). Table 5 presents mapped area as well as the sampling-based area estimates and associated uncertainties for the classes in the forest change maps from 1988 to 2022, calculated using the post-stratified estimator for area estimation and accuracy assessment, as recommended by Olofsson _et al_ (2014) (see also supplementary tables S13–S19). **Table 6.**Post-stratified area estimates and accuracies of each forest change class (1988–2022) after Olofsson _et al_ (2014).

results.title: Incorporating interpreter variability into estimation of the total variance of land cover area estimates under simple random sampling - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Incorporating interpreter variability into estimation of the total variance of land cover area estimates under simple random sampling. Area estimates of land cover and land cover change are often based on reference class labels determined by analysts interpreting satellite imagery and aerial photography. To evaluate the effect of interpreter variability on variance estimation, we used land cover reference data interpreted by seven analysts who each interpreted the same 300 sample pixels from a region of the Pacific Northwest of the United States. To avoid these problems of pixel counting, an unbiased estimator of area can be formulated using a probability sample and reference class labels interpreted for each sample unit, where these reference labels are assumed to be of better quality than the map data (Stehman, 2009; Olofsson et al., 2014). Example applications of sampling and use of reference class labels interpreted from remotely sensed data include estimating area of water (Pickens et al., 2020), cropland and cropland gain (Zalles et al., 2019), bare ground gain (Ying et al., 2017), forest disturbance (Cohen et al., 2016), forest change (Olofsson et al., 2010), fire (Boschetti et al., 2019), and “activity data” (i.e., area of human caused emissions used in the accounting of greenhouse gas emissions) (McRoberts et al., 2018). Interpreter variability contributes to the total variance of the estimator of area of a land cover class or area of type of land cover change, where the total variance includes both interpreter variance and sampling variance. The second and third objectives were accomplished by applying these variance estimators to sample data for which reference land cover interpretations were obtained by two analysts for the purpose of estimating area of land cover. The repeated measurements approach offers a practical way to incorporate both sampling variance and interpreter variance into an estimator of total variance for the estimated area of a land cover class. Application of the repeated measurements approach to the LCMAP pilot study land cover reference data interpreted for a simple random sample led to the following conclusions: (1) the contribution of reference data variability to the total variance can be substantial; (2) the usual variance.

results.title: Mitigating the effects of omission errors on area and area change estimates - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: Mitigating the effects of omission errors on area and area change estimates - ScienceDirect
Omissions of land change in maps can introduce large uncertainty in area estimates. In recent years, due largely to the inevitability of classification errors in remote sensing-based maps and the marked effects of these errors on subsequent area estimates, sample-based area estimates of land cover and land change have increased in importance and use. Errors of omission, defined as sample units observed as land change but mapped as a stable class, may introduce considerable uncertainty in parameter estimates obtained from the sample data (e.g., area estimates of land change). The effects of omission errors are exacerbated in situations where the area of intact forest is large relative to the area of forest change, a common situation in countries that seek results-based payments for reductions in deforestation and associated carbon emissions. While communicating statistically defensible estimates of areas of land cover and land change is of interest to the remote sensing community at large, the paradigm of area estimation has gained additional attention because of REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation) negotiated under the UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change). Still, at least up until 2010, bias and uncertainty were largely ignored in the remote sensing literature: an assessment of all articles related to mapping of land change published in *Remote Sensing of Environment* and *International Journal of Remote Sensing* for 2005–2010 showed that all but a few articles failed to include this information (Olofsson et al., 2013). (2014), which presents methods for estimating areas of land change and associated confidence intervals, and recommends the use of a map of land cover and land change to define strata for use with a stratified random sampling approach. Such omissions of land change in the map used to stratify the study area – characterized as *omission errors* – tend to carry large area weights and may result in area estimates with large uncertainty that are very different from mapped areas. Omission errors – especially sample units observed as land change that occur in larger strata corresponding to stable land cover classes – have been shown to have a profound adverse effect on area estimates.

results.title: Optimizing sample size allocation to strata for estimating area and map accuracy - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Optimizing sample size allocation to strata for estimating area and map accuracy. In this article, the allocation that minimizes the sum of the variances of the estimators of user's accuracy, producer's accuracy, and area of a single targeted class for a fixed total sample size is derived for stratified random sampling. Practitioners can apply these optimization results to guide sample size allocation decisions when using a stratified random sampling design for accuracy assessment and area estimation. In this article we derive an optimal sample allocation to strata when the objectives of the accuracy assessment are to estimate user's accuracy, producer's accuracy, and proportion of area of a single targeted class of primary interest. Optimizing the sample allocation for the accuracy and area estimates of all classes is not addressed. That is, we assume that the class listed as row *i* = 1 and column *j* = 1 in the error matrix (Table 1) is the primary class of interest, and the optimal allocation of the total sample to the strata is constructed to minimize the sum of the variances of the estimators of user's accuracy of map class 1, producer's accuracy of reference class 1, and proportion of area of reference class 1. The optimal allocation we implement in this article differs from previous studies in that the optimization targets three specific estimates of primary interest, user's accuracy, producer's accuracy, and proportion of area for a single high priority class. Optimal allocation results are illustrated for 2 × 2 and 4 × 4 error matrices, where for each example the optimization minimizes the sum of the variances of the estimators of user's accuracy of class 1 in the error matrix, producer's accuracy of class 1, and proportion of area of class 1. (2014) provide some ad hoc guidelines for sample allocation when the objectives are to estimate accuracy and area, and Wagner and Stehman (2015) provide a spreadsheet program for objectively determining the optimal allocation that simultaneously minimizes the sum of the variances of the estimates of user's accuracy, producer's accuracy, and area (based on the reference classification) of a single target class.
